scenario: Today's main thread in this track is trimming robot policies and checking where their high scores come from. One paper uses training-free nearest-neighbor retrieval to score close to mainstream VLAs on LIBERO, showing that much of the high score comes from looking up demonstrations. APS-VLA keeps only the visual tokens that help actions, and MetaWAM puts all robot signals into a single frame, both cutting latency without changing the backbone architecture. CIALLO and DexSeed find ways to make one set of demonstrations serve more robots and objects. LEASH and NTT's world model focus on the moment before acting: check the scene for safety first, or rehearse the outcome before choosing an action.

papers.title: From Video Frames to Robot Meta-Frames: A Unified Latent Interface for World Action Models
papers.authors: Guoqiang Liang, Yiqi Lin, Yanzhe Chen, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Mike Zheng Shou
papers.abstract: Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations. Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g. proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders. We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem: how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising. Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less. Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change. A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables. On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks. Code and models are available at https://github.com/showlab/MetaWAM
papers.summary: When a video diffusion model is turned into a robot world action model, low-dimensional signals such as joint state, actions and value must enter a latent space that has only seen natural video. The usual fix gives each signal its own frame, which lengthens the sequence and the attention cost. The authors first probe a frozen denoiser: signals tiled directly across the frame need large corrections, so they sit far from the video distribution, while signals packed in the frequency domain and mapped back by an inverse DCT need the smallest corrections. MetaWAM therefore splits all robot signals into separate frequency bands inside a single frame, with no new modules. On RoboCasa it reaches 68.9% success and cuts inference latency by 39%. ==How a signal is laid out in the latent space matters more than how many slots it takes.== Putting user behavior, IDs and other structured signals into an LLM token sequence raises the same question.

papers.title: APS-VLA: Action-Guided and Future-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Xiaoyang Xing, Chun-Mei Feng, Anthony Cohn, Xiaoliang Gong, Asoke Nandi
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $\pi_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.
papers.summary: A VLA processes hundreds of visual tokens at every step, which makes inference slow, yet the next action often depends on a small part of the image. This paper adds a small scorer in front of a frozen VLA and learns from demonstration trajectories which tokens to keep. Training asks two things: the kept tokens must let the original model produce the same action it gives with the full image, and together with the demonstrated actions they must predict how the image changes a few steps later. At deployment the scorer selects once, and the original model's weights and action generation stay unchanged. On LIBERO, pruning 75% of visual tokens makes inference 1.57 times faster while success is only 1.25 points below the unpruned model. Pruning harder barely adds speed but makes success fall faster. ==Which tokens to keep depends on whether they help the next actions and visual changes==, not only on how similar they are to the instruction. It is the same idea as learning feature selection from the downstream objective in recommendation.

papers.title: CIALLO: Learning Shared Intent Representations for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
papers.authors: Choo Sin Wai, Dake Zhong, Jingye Zhang, Zhifang Liu, Siyao Xiao, Zirong Ding, Yuhong Zhang, Kangjie Chen, Dongbin Zhang, Guorui Song, Guocun Wang, Peng Jiao, Haoqian Wang
papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7\% average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0\% for fully finetuned $\pi_0$. In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3\% success on LIBERO and 52.7\% on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8\% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning.
papers.summary: Robots write actions in different ways, some as joint angles and some as end-effector displacements, so one robot's demonstrations are hard to reuse on another. This paper trains an action codec that aligns actions, the change between two frames and the instruction in one space, which represents the intended motion over the next short stretch of time. Each robot's body differences live only in a small set of its own embeddings, so a new robot needs one recording of at most 10 seconds and about half an hour to update that set. A large model is then trained to predict the intent from images and instructions with only a few demonstrations per task, reaching 76.7% average success on two new real robots, compared with 70.0% for a fully finetuned off-the-shelf robot model. ==Separating body calibration from task learning lets a new robot get by with very little data.== It resembles the recommendation pattern of a shared representation plus a small set of parameters per scenario.

papers.title: ReACT: Reflection-Consistent Modulation and Cross-Load Consistency for Humanoid Velocity Tracking Under Asymmetric Loads
papers.authors: Xianghui Wang, Aoran Fu, Liyou Luo, Shanze Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Dan Zhang, Wei Zhang
papers.abstract: In recent years, humanoid loco-manipulation has progressed to whole-body grasping, lifting, and transport. A basic requirement underlying these tasks is carrying the object to its destination, which depends on the locomotion controller accurately executing velocity commands from the navigation policy. However, carrying an object in one hand introduces a persistent asymmetric upper-body load that can degrade velocity tracking. Persistent tracking biases can accumulate into position and heading deviations, increasing the risk of collisions and navigation failure. To address this problem, we present ReACT, a framework for accurate velocity tracking under asymmetric upper-body loads. Reflection-consistent disturbance modulation uses the estimated wrench to modulate actor features for load compensation while preserving action correspondence under reflected observations. Cross-load tracking consistency training compares loaded and unloaded conditions under the same velocity commands to promote consistent velocity tracking across loading conditions. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot show improved velocity tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads. Real-world experiments demonstrate collision-free goal reaching in all 40 tested navigation trials under unilateral hand loads with a fixed mapless navigation policy.
papers.summary: When a humanoid walks with an object in one hand, the uneven load makes it drift sideways and slowly turn off course, until it may hit obstacles. This paper trains the walking policy with three copies of the environment running together, empty-handed, loaded on the left and loaded on the right, all given the same velocity command. Each copy is penalized by how far its displacement and heading stray from the average of the three. The policy also adjusts its internal features from the estimated external force, while guaranteeing that mirrored observations produce mirrored actions. In simulation, its turning-rate tracking error is more than 80% lower than that of the FALCON baseline. On the real robot, carrying 1.5 kg in one hand during mapless navigation, it reaches the goal without collision in all 40 trials, while FALCON fails every trial through collisions. ==Comparing the same command under different loads side by side directly suppresses the bias.== In recommendation, too, such paired consistency constraints are more direct than simply adding perturbations.

papers.title: DexSeed: Expanding Human Hand-Object Interactions into Robot Demonstrations for Dexterous Policy Learning
papers.authors: Huaijin Pi, Zehong Shen, Yong Wang, Kechun Xu, Changpeng Wang, Dingkun Wei, Xueyang Wang, Wenjia Wang, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Taku Komura
papers.abstract: We study how to generate diverse, physically executable robot demonstrations for dexterous vision-language-action (VLA) learning. Existing demonstration-generation methods typically rely on costly teleoperated examples. Meanwhile, human hand--object datasets provide a reusable source, but existing transfer methods mainly reproduce given interactions. Turning these interactions into VLA training data further requires coverage of different objects and manipulation locations, together with executable arm and finger actions, and visual observations. To achieve this, we present DexSeed, a framework for low-cost generation of dexterous robot data from human hand--object interactions. Our key idea is to expand human sequences while preserving their grasps and realizing the resulting motions under arm-tracking dynamics in physics simulation. Specifically, we organize source sequences by grasp mode with shared language descriptions. InteractionMesh-based retargeting and arm trajectory augmentation adapt these sequences to the robot hand, different object geometries, and pick-and-place locations while preserving local hand--object relationships. An RL finger-control policy produces executable rollouts, while the arm tracks precomputed trajectories. Rendered observations and recorded actions from successful rollouts are paired with grasp descriptions to fine-tune a VLA. Experiments show improved contact fidelity in retargeting and more reliable whole-arm execution than the evaluated baselines. Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment further demonstrate that a VLA fine-tuned solely on the generated demonstrations can execute language-specified grasps. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/DexSeed/.
papers.summary: Dexterous-hand demonstrations are expensive, because teleoperation has to coordinate many finger joints at once. This paper starts from existing human grasp data, groups it by grasp type, transfers each human hand motion to a robot hand, and then varies object shape, start position and placement to expand it into many demonstrations. The key step is training finger control in physics simulation with the robot arm included. A version trained with a floating hand succeeds almost every time on its own, but once the arm's tracking errors come in its success falls below 30%, while putting the arm in the training loop raises it to 95.50%. In the end 19 human sequences yield 25270 demonstrations, and a VLA finetuned only on this data performs all eight grasp types on a real robot when asked in language. ==Demonstrations used without physical verification teach the policy almost nothing.== The same holds when rules or simulators generate training samples: run them in an environment with real constraints first and keep only the successful ones.

papers.title: How Much of Your VLA Is kNN
papers.authors: Denis Grachev, Damien LaRocque, Omar Moured
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.
papers.summary: Mainstream VLAs now exceed 95% success on LIBERO, but how much of that is real generalization? The authors build a training-free control: take the current image, find the most similar frames in the demonstration set, and directly execute a weighted average of the actions that followed them, which already reaches 91.7% success. On the perturbed LIBERO-Plus, this retrieval policy loses less than every VLA tested. The authors then use the vision-language backbones of nine public VLAs as retrieval vectors and find that finetuning mainly turns the backbone into a better retrieval vector, while the actions the VLAs output stay close to the demonstrations. ==On a benchmark with demonstrations this dense, much of the high score can be had by lookup.== Recommendation engineers know this well: report a nearest-neighbor baseline next to the complex model, and only then do you know what the model actually learned.

papers.title: DexForesight: Grounding Dexterous Policies with Implicit Spatial Foresight
papers.authors: Zhongxi Chen, Yi Yang, Xinyi Chen, Mingzhe Ye, Yaping Li
papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation requires rich spatial foresight over both the surrounding scene and the robot hand. Existing world-action models often acquire such predictive knowledge through explicit future prediction. We introduce DexForesight, a framework that learns spatial foresight implicitly by injecting dynamics-aware world representations into the latent space of a dexterous policy. During training, DexForesight learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from offline scene depth, kinematic hand geometry, and demonstration trajectories. The world model predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, capturing both articulated hand dynamics and scene changes under demonstrated actions, including the motion of fingers occluded from the cameras. We then freeze the world model and align policy queries with its predictive world queries, transferring the learned spatial dynamics into policy latents and using them to condition action generation. At deployment, only the policy is retained, operating on RGB observations, language, and robot state without depth input or explicit future prediction. On 11 DexJoCo simulation tasks, DexForesight improves the overall success rate of the base policy from 49.4% to 60.5%. On three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks, DexForesight achieves 58.3% success, compared with 50.0% for the strongest baseline. Project page https://dexforesight.github.io/
papers.summary: Dexterous manipulation needs foresight about how the fingers and objects will move next, and many methods get it through explicit future prediction. During training, this paper first learns an action-conditioned world model. It uses scene depth, hand geometry and demonstration trajectories to predict the 3D motion of points on the hand and the change in image features, including fingers the cameras cannot see. It then freezes this model and aligns the policy's internal representations with the world model's predictive ones, transferring the foresight into the policy. At deployment only the policy remains, taking just RGB images, language and robot state, with no depth input and no future prediction. On 11 simulated dexterous tasks, overall success rises from 49.4% to 60.5%. ==Foresight can be taught to the policy during training, with no need to generate the future at inference.== It matches the recommendation practice of training with a teacher that sees future information and serving only the student.

papers.title: LEASH: Stay Safe in Agentic Robotics
papers.authors: Qinfeng Zhu, Weiguang Zhao, Ke Sun, Xihao Guo, Yunxi Jiang, Rui Zhang, Lei Fan, Kaizhu Huang
papers.abstract: Foundation models such as GPT and Claude have shown strong capabilities in spatial understanding and embodied intelligence. These advances make agentic robotics a promising path toward artificial general intelligence in robotics. However, we find that using foundation models to control robots poses serious safety risks, and comprehensive safety evaluation is still lacking. We introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety in agentic robotics. Its 92 simulated tasks and 13 physical-robot tasks fall into five categories: Task-level Refusal (T), Plan Repair (P), Execution-time Hazard (E), Injection (I), and Sequential Memory (S). Prior benchmarks cover at most two of these categories, and several evaluate only text outputs. In contrast, RoboRisk covers all five and executes every task in closed loop. We evaluate six state-of-the-art foundation models on RoboRisk: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and Grok 4.7. These models generally show high harm rates. We also evaluate two robot-specific APIs: the Dream API and PokeBot's RoboAPI. We further propose the Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness (LEASH), which offers essential safety infrastructure for agentic robotics and can be integrated into nearly any agentic architecture. LEASH leverages a decision model (Jev or OpenAI's Decisions API) to implement task, action, and commit gates, which review the task, each action, and each irreversible operation in their visual context. The planner and all three gates share a common safety policy. Experiments on RoboRisk in simulation and on physical robots show that LEASH effectively reduces harm across all six foundation models. It largely preserves their task completion performance and adds little time and token overhead.
papers.summary: Letting large models control a robot arm directly produces concrete hazards, such as dropping a phone into a bowl of water or carrying milk over a power strip. The authors build a robot safety benchmark covering five kinds of risk, from instructions that should be refused to injected instructions hidden in the scene. Every task runs in closed loop in simulation and on a real robot, and mainstream models commonly cause harm. Their fix adds three gates around an existing agent: before a task starts, before each action, and before irreversible operations such as opening the gripper or pouring, a fast scoring model judges from the current camera images whether it is safe. The planner and all three gates read the same safety rules. With the gates, the harm rate of one of the best baseline models in simulation drops from 11.23% to 0, and end-to-end time grows by only 1.66% on average. ==Safety review for robots has to look at the scene, not only the instruction text.== Engineers building agent systems can borrow this layered review.

papers.title: Can AI agents program industrial robots without training data? Berkeley says yes
papers.abstract:
UC Berkeley and NVIDIA have released open-source tools for teams of AI coding agents that write, simulate, and refine readable robot programs. 

The post Can AI agents program industrial robots without training data? Berkeley says yes appeared first on The Robot Report.
papers.summary: Programming, tuning and troubleshooting industrial robots has taken weeks to months, and the work has to wait until the whole workcell is installed. UC Berkeley and NVIDIA have released open-source tools that let a team of coding agents write robot programs themselves, test them in simulation, see where they fail and revise, without first collecting large amounts of data. The core idea splits a task into a graph of nodes such as perception, grasp planning and collision-free motion, with each node assigned to its own agent so they work in parallel without interfering. The output is Python code that engineers can read, calling existing vendor modules for low-level drive control rather than replacing the robot controller. The Newton physics engine used for simulation has hundreds of parameters, so the team built an interface with sliders that lets the agents tune it on their own. ==Because the output is readable code, engineers can check it piece by piece before deployment.== For recommendation and search engineers, it is like having agents write reviewable rules and pipelines instead of training yet another black-box model.

papers.title: NTT Develops Physical AI Technology That Predicts the Future Before Robots Move to Prevent Failures
papers.abstract: Physics-based world model predicts load collapse and object drops, advancing automated loading and unloading of diverse items such as airport baggage.
papers.summary: When robots load baggage or stack goods, the main fear is a stack collapsing or an item falling, and existing control programs alone can hardly tell in advance. NTT rehearses before acting: for each candidate action from the control program, a world model generates a video of what will happen next, scores whether the load will collapse or drop, and the most promising action is executed. This world model attaches a physics module to a video generation model, which estimates each object's position, velocity and mass from the video and computes its next motion from the equations of motion. The result guides video generation, so objects rarely vanish or deform and situations missing from the training data can be handled. In a shelf-loading task where a small robot simulates stacking items, success rises from 73.1% to 92.3%. ==Computing physical quantities explicitly makes the generated future reliable and the basis of the judgment visible.== It is the same as scoring candidates in a simulator before launch in recommendation.
